claims.text: The initial material consists of equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles smaller than 10 nm.
The initial nanoparticles have an FCC multi-twinned or icosahedral structure.
The nanoparticles were synthesized by pulsed laser deposition at 873 K on a silicon nitride membrane.
The proposed intervention heats the nanoparticles from 298 K to 973 K at 1 K/s under vacuum.
Surface-energy differences drive active atomic diffusion and migration of Au and Cu to the nanoparticle surface.
Nanoparticle reshaping or coalescence accelerates local atomic diffusion.
Surface-segregated Au and Cu undergo local melting or evaporation during heating.
Evaporation of Au and Cu decreases particle size and compromises structural and chemical integrity.
The smallest nanoparticles, particularly those 2–4 nm in size, will progressively disappear during heating.
Heating will widen the nanoparticle size distribution.
Heating will reduce the average particle size through evaporation of surface-segregated Au and Cu.
Heating will produce a transition from elliptical or multi-twinned particles toward more spherical particles.
High-entropy stabilization and sluggish diffusion would otherwise be expected to preserve the initial particle size and structure during heating.
Diffusion and segregation effects become prominent above approximately 673 K.
The outcome depends on nanoparticle shape, including whether particles are icosahedral or truncated octahedral.
The proposed instability is most significant for particles smaller than 10 nm.
